html:
Jagadish Chandra Bose was the first modern scientist of India to win a world name. He did early work on radio waves and then showed that plants respond to the world much as animals do.

He was born in Bengal in 1858, studied at Cambridge and in 1885 became professor of physics at Presidency College, Calcutta. Indians were paid a third less than Europeans. He taught for three years without drawing any salary until the college gave him equal pay.

In a small room he built his own equipment and from 1894 made and studied very short radio waves, a few millimetres long. In 1895, in Calcutta's town hall, he sent waves through walls to ring a bell and set off gunpowder. Marconi's first signals came the same year. Bose used a crystal of galena as a detector and patented it in 1904, the first patent for a semiconductor device. He had no wish to make money from his work and published it freely.

After 1900 he turned to plants. His crescograph magnified growth ten thousand times. With it he recorded how plants react to heat, cold, light, poison and injury.

He founded the Bose Institute in Calcutta in 1917. The physicist S. N. Bose was his student.
